Distributions 1: Evaluating and Sampling¶

A distribution answers four questions about a variable: how dense is the probability at a point (pdf), how much probability lies below it (cdf), what are their logarithms (logpdf, logcdf), and what do random draws from it look like (sample). Here every such function works on a whole Series at once, so a grid of a million points is one call. After this chapter you can evaluate and draw from any of the sixty families, keep accuracy far in the tails, give each point its own parameters, and look up a family’s parameters in the table below.

Every program is complete and its output is the output of that program.

Two ways in¶

Distribution objects. The common families are structs holding their parameters, with the same methods: Normal{mean, stddev}, Lognormal{mean_log, stddev_log}, Uniform{low, high}, Exponential{rate}, Laplace{location, scale}, Logistic{location, scale}, Rayleigh{sigma}, Gamma{shape, scale, location}, ChiSquare{degrees_of_freedom}, InverseGaussian{theta, chi} (mean and shape), StudentT{degrees_of_freedom, location, scale}, FDistribution{numerator, denominator}, Weibull{shape, scale}, Beta{low, high, alpha, beta}, NormalTrunc{lower, upper, mean, stddev}, Nig and Gh (Chapter 3), and the discrete Bernoulli{p}, Binomial{count, p}, Poisson{lambda}, Geometric{p}, NegativeBinomial{r, p}, Skellam{lambda1, lambda2}. For a discrete family pdf is the probability mass function (a count k outside the support has probability 0).

Method

Result

pdf(x), logpdf(x)

density (mass) and its logarithm

cdf(x), logcdf(x)

distribution function and its logarithm

sample(sizes, cfg, seed), sample_like(like, seed)

random draws (Chapter below)

cgf(t), cumulant(order)

cumulant generating function, and the cumulant of a given order (the first is the mean, the second the variance)

MLE(x)

maximum likelihood fit (Chapter 2)

By kind. All families, including the less common ones, are reached through dst::Kind values (dst::Weibull, dst::StudentT, dst::Yule …) and the free functions pdf(kind, x, params), logpdf, cdf, sample(kind, params, sizes, cfg, seed) and sample_like(kind, params, like, seed), with params a list of the parameters in the order of the table. supports(kind) tells whether a kind is implemented. The namespace aliases used in the programs are namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr; and namespace dst = distr::dst;.

Accuracy¶

The densities and distribution functions are accurate to rounding over the usual range and far into the tails, where the logarithmic forms matter: cdf of a normal rounds to exactly 0 below about −38, logcdf carries on (−1805 at −60). The densities of the normal inverse Gaussian and generalised hyperbolic families use the modified Bessel function of the second kind of any real order, evaluated to about 12 digits (it is also exact in its logarithm for large arguments).

Parameters as Series¶

Any parameter of an object may be a Series instead of a number. The points and the parameters are then paired element by element, so one call evaluates a different distribution at every point: this is how a model with a mean and a variance per observation is evaluated.

Random draws¶

sample({n}) draws n independent values; sample({rows, cols}, cfg, seed) fills an array of any shape; sample_like(like) matches the shape, dtype and platform of an existing array. A given seed always produces the same numbers (a seed of 0 is a fixed default, not a random one); different seeds give different, independent streams. cfg selects the dtype and platform of the result (default: Float32 on the CPU).

Checklist¶

  1. Use logpdf and logcdf for anything that is multiplied or compared far in the tails; the plain forms underflow.

  2. Pass the parameters in the order of the table (the long form of the gamma is {location, scale, shape}).

  3. Give a seed whenever a result must be reproducible; use a different seed for each independent stream.

  4. Use sample_like to match the shape, dtype and device of an array you already have.

  5. Use Series parameters to evaluate one distribution per point in a single call.
